Because of the gambling-like atmosphere in the world today, I found myself reacting to 'Expect a return of 100,000 fold' (MN 142.6) to feel like ranking or selfish expectation. Can you expand on the true meaning?
AN 7.22.4: Transactional giving.
This morning you spoke about giving gifts to yourself like silence and relaxation...
You feel this safety being around people who are following the precepts, and that's such a gift to everybody.
The meaning of Abhayagiri.

In Masons, when they do a good deed, they're not supposed to tell anybody about it. That keeps your ego in check. Is there anything like that in the Dhamma? Did the Buddha speak to anonymity when we give? Or is it part of the training to teach yourself to put your ego aside [when recognized]?
Could you speak to the skillfulness of generosity when it comes from insecurity, wanting to belong, or wanting to be liked?
Sometimes when I help people I feel happy and other times I feel nothing. Am I supposed to feel happy? Am I expecting too much?
AN 3.34: Timescales of the results of action.

I don't expect much from people, but when I do something not good, I want to kill myself and lose sleep. I feel like I should do more and more in terms of meditation, making offerings, and the way I treat people.
In Mahāyana tradition, it says there is no giver, no gift, no receiver, and ultimately everything is empty. Is this the same as giving gifts without any attachment or asking anything in return?
Don't be an arahant, don't be a Bodhisattva, don't be anything at all.|Ajahn Chah

I always enjoy coming [to Abhayagiri] and the questions and answers in Berkeley because it's such a happy place. I volunteer at a homeless ministry in the Tenderloin in San Francisco, and it's not a happy place. The leaders are ex-Franciscan nuns. Their faith is very strong in the face of suffering, and that's what inspires me to participate in an environment that's frightening, dangerous, and unwholesome. The inspiration of being around others who have faith helps me to go beyond my own life experience, and this seems like a very important part of the ability to give.

In Thai we do the (??? Thai phrase) for our [deceased] parents. How can we know they really see our words, the dedication, the dana, the goodness that we try to do? They might be reborn in a different life. What are your thoughts on that?
